name: The Nature Conservancy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. PRANA's crop-burning deaths in northwest India (48%); forest and land carbon, power displaced and pandemic risk, spread by world population (41%); adaptation's coastal people in Mexico and Hawai'i (6%, split by judgment); the fisheries rules' fishers in the Seychelles and the Pacific islands (3%, split by judgment); the year's deals' local incomes in Ecuador and The Bahamas (2%, by their people).
summary: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) buys and protects land and water in the US and about 80 countries, brokers debt-for-nature deals with governments, and works on clean energy, food systems, fresh water and fisheries. We model all of its fiscal year 2025 spending (July 2024 to June 2025, $1.28 billion of conservation programmes and land purchases), each of its nine pathways from the research on its kind of work, in 13 branches: forest kept by the Ecuador Amazon deal, the land it bought and its protection policy; power displaced by mine-land solar and renewable siting maps; Pará's deforestation-free cattle rule, zero-conversion soy in the Gran Chaco, regenerative farming and the PRANA no-burn programme in India; restoration; fisheries rules; and climate adaptation. The result is about 0.0004 years of healthy life per $1,000, under a tenth of the site's climate models, because most of TNC's work keeps land carbon, which is worth little in healthy years, and TNC is a small share of the resources behind its large deals, rules and policies. Nearly half of it is the air-pollution deaths averted by less crop burning in Punjab and Haryana, most of whose fall would have come anyway; a third is the Pará cattle rule, mostly through the least grounded step, a small cut in pandemic risk from forest kept, and its roll-out has barely begun. Every branch rests on thin data and is discounted for missing data, and the result is mostly uncertainty (combined range about 0.00005-0.0035).

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Conservation programme spending modelled: every pathway, FY2025
rows.explainer: All of TNC's conservation spending in its fiscal year 2025 (July 2024 to June 2025): the activities of its nine pathways plus the land it bought. Every pathway is modelled below as a branch of this model (Convention 4), so nothing is left out and no part of the budget is set against another part's outcomes. TNC publishes no split by pathway (its Form 990 reports one programme line, $947.6 million in FY2024, and says a split wouldn't reflect how it spends), so each branch's outcome is for its whole pathway and the branches share this one cost.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: hectares of new protection the year's deal finances

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Ecuador announces debt conversion for Amazon conservation (15 December 2024)
source.quote: protect an additional 1.8 million hectares of forests and wetlands

rows.explainer: TNC's largest land deal of the year: Ecuador's debt conversion for the Amazon Biocorridor Program, closed in December 2024 (FY2025) with TNC's Nature Bonds Program, finances new protection of 1.8 million hectares of forests and wetlands over 17 years. Other big deals fall outside the year: Eternal Mongolia was signed in April 2024 (FY2024) and the Cochamó purchase in Chile closed in December 2025 (FY2026). The year's ocean deals (The Bahamas, 6.8 million hectares of marine protected areas, November 2024; the Seychelles marine spatial plan signed into law in 2025) store no counted carbon and enter through the livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: hectares of existing protected areas whose management the deal improves

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Ecuador announces debt conversion for Amazon conservation (15 December 2024)
source.quote: improve the management of 4.6 million hectares of existing protected areas

rows.explainer: Existing protected areas the same programme funds better management of (rangers, plans, community agreements).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon: hectares counted (new protections plus better management at its weight)
Ecuador Amazon deal: people whose incomes the protection changes
rows.explainer: Indigenous and other communities in and around the Ecuadorian Biocorridor, a share of the Ecuadorian Amazon's roughly one million people. TNC publishes no count; our guess is 100,000 people (20,000-400,000).

rows.label: The year's ocean deals: fishers and coastal people whose incomes the marine plans change
rows.explainer: The Bahamas' debt conversion (6.8 million hectares of marine protected areas under better management, November 2024) sets fishing rules and no-take zones; its fishing and tourism communities are tens of thousands of people. Our guess is 30,000 (5,000-100,000). The Seychelles' fishers are counted once, in the fisheries branch (its 2025 fisheries law), not here.

rows.label: People whose incomes the year's deals change
Average price TNC pays per hectare of land or easement
rows.explainer: TNC doesn't publish the hectares it bought in the year, only what it paid. Our guess at the average price, $5,000 a hectare ($2,000-15,000), is anchored on US rural land values (USDA's 2024 Land Values survey puts pasture at about $1,800 an acre, about $4,400 a hectare, and cropland near $5,500 an acre); easements cost less than fee purchases, land near cities and coasts much more.

rows.label: Land bought: hectares (purchases ÷ average price)
Wellbeing: people who visit or live with the protected nature
rows.explainer: 0 at the best guess: visitors to the newly bought land mostly would have gone to other nature nearby, and the Amazon and ocean areas get few visitors. The range allows up to 50,000 people a year whose life satisfaction gains.

rows.label: Protection policy: tropical forest hectares whose new protection or secure tenure the year's policy work advances
rows.explainer: Two of TNC's nine pathways (natural climate solutions; transformative management and protection) support national 30x30 commitments, Indigenous land tenure and forest policy beyond the deals of the Nature Bonds and Enduring Earth teams. TNC reports no hectares for them in the year. Our guess, 1 million hectares a year (0.2-5 million), is anchored on the deal branch: one large deal (Ecuador) brought 1.8 million new hectares and 4.6 million better managed; policy work moves larger areas more weakly, which the attribution and implementation rows below carry. Tropical forest only: grassland, ocean and temperate land under these pathways are a positive share in prot_unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Clean energy: CO₂ the Neyveli mine-land solar project avoids over its life (TNC's figure)

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Annual Report 2025
source.quote: Over its lifetime, the project will avoid the equivalent of 1.17 million metric tons of CO2 emissions

rows.explainer: India's first solar project on reclaimed mine land, supported by TNC's Mining the Sun initiative, came online in September 2025. TNC's own estimate of its lifetime emissions avoided: the project's output, not what TNC caused (that is the counterfactual and attribution rows).

rows.label: Clean energy: homes the year's 17 Appalachian mine-land projects can power

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Annual Report 2025
source.quote: In 2025 alone, TNC and partners announced plans for 17 clean energy projects in Virginia, Kentucky and Tennessee—enough to power more than 6,000 Appalachian homes.

rows.explainer: Projects announced in 2025 with utilities and communities on retired coal mines; announced, not yet built (energy_implementation_adj).

rows.label: Siting maps: renewable capacity planned in the year with siting maps TNC helped make
rows.explainer: TNC's mapping tools guide renewables planning in nine Indian states; it helped Croatia publish biodiversity sensitivity maps and drafted a siting blueprint for nine Eastern European countries with the Energy Community, and is launching national maps in Portugal, Montenegro and Romania (annual report 2025, pp. 8-9). No capacity is reported. India adds about 25-30 GW of solar and wind a year, Croatia about 1; our guess is that 3 GW a year (0.5-15) is planned in zones TNC's maps shaped.

rows.label: Foodscapes: cropland newly under regenerative practices in the year (cover crops, no-till)
rows.explainer: TNC's foodscapes in the US Corn Belt and Chesapeake, Kenya and elsewhere, and its new Regenerative Foodscapes Accelerator (Provide FY25 review), report goals rather than hectares; the Upper Tana fund put 450,000 acres (180,000 hectares) of farmland under better practice over ten years, about 18,000 a year. With the US programmes, our guess is 50,000 hectares a year (10,000-300,000).

rows.label: PRANA: farmers who have adopted no-burn practices (northwest India, to 2025)

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Provide Food & Water Global Priority: 2025 Year in Review
source.quote: To date, PRANA has enabled 300,000 farmers across more than 6,000 villages to adopt no-burn practices.

rows.explainer: TNC's own count for its Promoting Regenerative and No-burn Agriculture programme in Punjab and Haryana, launched in 2021; not independently audited (prana_implementation_adj).

rows.label: PRANA: cropland targeted for no burning

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Provide Food & Water Global Priority: 2025 Year in Review
source.quote: Eliminate burning on 500,000 hectares of cropland and 150,000 hectares on improved rice management

rows.label: PRANA: farmers targeted

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Provide Food & Water Global Priority: 2025 Year in Review
source.quote: Support at least 220,000 farmers to adopt no-burn and improved rice management practices

rows.label: PRANA: cropland per farmer
rows.explainer: The programme's own targets, 500,000 hectares for 220,000 farmers: about 2.3 hectares each (Punjab's average holding is larger, about 3.6 hectares).

rows.label: Restoration: hectares replanted or regrowing from the year's work (water funds, forests, wetlands)
rows.explainer: Hectares replanted or left to regrow (forests, riparian strips, wetlands, mangroves) by the fresh-water and adaptation pathways and on TNC's own preserves. Thinning and prescribed burns, much of the water funds' forest work (the Rio Grande Water Fund's 'more than 100,000 hectares' in 10 years are acres of thinning and burns, about 250,000 acres or 100,000 hectares), take up no regrowth carbon; their fire protection is a positive share in rest_unmodelled_benefits_adj. Other anchors: the Upper Tana fund planted 5.5 million trees in 10 years (a few thousand hectares), the Bogotá and Cape Town funds restore catchments. TNC publishes no yearly total; our guess is 30,000 hectares a year of regrowth (10,000-150,000).

rows.label: Fisheries: fishers and fishing-community members whose fishery the year's binding rules change
rows.explainer: The year's binding rules (Provide FY25 review, pp. 23-24): the Seychelles' Fisheries and Aquaculture Act (Act 3 of 2025, passed by the National Assembly on 14 May 2025) made electronic monitoring legally required on fishing vessels in a tuna sector worth nearly a quarter of its GDP; all four tuna regional fisheries bodies adopted minimum monitoring standards; Pacific Island Tuna Provisions extended its sourcing standards. Monitoring deters illegal fishing, which over years leaves more fish for the small-scale and coastal fishers who share the stocks. Chile's planned limits for 17 coastal species are for recreational fishing, and the Amazon fisheries map is a monitoring tool, so neither is counted. TNC publishes no count of people; our guess is 50,000 (10,000-200,000).

rows.label: Adaptation: coastal people whose flood and storm protection the year's reef, mangrove and insurance work improves
rows.explainer: The adaptation pathway's projects in the year (annual report 2025, pp. 4-7): parametric reef insurance and reef brigades along Mexico's Quintana Roo coast and the first US reef insurance for Hawai'i, wildfire insurance in California, mangrove restoration with coastal communities. TNC's goal is to help 100 million people at severe climate risk by 2030 but it reports no count for the year; the coasts behind the insured reefs hold hundreds of thousands of people. Our guess is 300,000 (50,000-2 million).

rows.label: People whose health the protection changes directly (counted in PRANA instead)
rows.explainer: 0: the one health effect with a dose (the smoke of crop burning) is counted as deaths averted in the PRANA branch, valued by age like every death. Water-fund and green-space health effects are positive shares in the branches' unmodelled-benefits rows.

rows.label: Wild animal-years affected (none counted)
rows.explainer: 0: TNC claims no welfare effect on wild animals, and more animals alive is not by itself a gain (conservation family). The sign is unknown.

rows.label: Years a won deal, rule or policy counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for a won deal or reform (normalization.md 2.9): the years TNC's work brought the change forward, not how long it lasts. Used by every branch that wins something (the deals, land bought, protection policy, clean-energy siting, the cattle rule, fisheries rules). Whether the change would have come anyway is these years, so the branches' counterfactual rows ask only what share of the loss or harm the change prevents (Convention 5).

rows.label: Wait until a new protection starts avoiding forest loss
rows.explainer: The Ecuador programme declares its new protections and builds management over its first years (it is funded over 17), so the avoided loss starts on average about three years after the year's spending (1-8). Protection policy (the prot branch) is assumed to take as long. Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years of protection, discounted (deals and protection policy)
rows.explainer: Every year of protection, and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Share of the forest loss a protected area prevents

source.title: ScienceDaily (Oregon State University), Formal protected area designation reduces the rate of deforestation but does not prevent it; Wolf et al. (2021), Nature Ecology & Evolution
source.quote: They found protected areas' deforestation rate is 41% lower than that of unprotected areas.

rows.explainer: The share of the forest loss expected without protection that protection prevents: from a matched comparison of more than 18,000 protected-area parcels (Wolf et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution, doi 10.1038/s41559-021-01389-0) with similar unprotected land (elevation, slope, nearness to people). Protection slows forest loss but doesn't stop it. The range is ours (20-60%), for the spread between regions and between strict and multiple-use areas. It is the counterfactual of the deal and protection-policy branches (deal_counterfactual_adj, prot_counterfactual_adj), applied there once: the tonnes in the reach and effect rows are the forest at risk, before protection (one question per adjustment).

rows.label: Tropical primary forest lost worldwide in 2023

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: Total tropical primary forest loss in 2023 totaled 3.7 million hectares

rows.explainer: With the next row, the CO₂ released per hectare of tropical primary forest lost; also the denominator of the catastrophic-risk branch.

rows.label: CO₂ released by that loss

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: All this forest loss produced 2.4 gigatonnes (Gt) of carbon dioxide emissions in 2023

rows.explainer: Gross emissions from the year's tropical primary forest loss.

rows.label: Tropical forest: CO₂ released per hectare of primary forest lost
rows.explainer: 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares: about 650 tonnes a hectare, the tropics' average, used for the Ecuadorian Amazon, protection policy and Pará.

rows.label: Climate: CO₂ a year at risk on those hectares, before protection (average, for reading only)
rows.explainer: The emissions the deal's and the bought land's hectares would release a year without protection (loss rate × CO₂ per hectare lost), averaged over them. The share protection prevents is not in this figure: it is in each branch's counterfactual row, so a hectare that would be lost anyway is counted once (conservation family pitfall).

rows.label: Effect of better management of an existing protected area, relative to new protection
rows.explainer: A hectare already protected on paper loses less forest than an unprotected one, so funding its management prevents less loss than a new protection. Our guess is a quarter of a new protection's effect (10-50%), anchored on the protected-area effect below (deforestation 41% lower in protected areas): if unfunded paper parks deliver about half of a funded park's effect, better management adds the other half of a smaller remaining gap.

rows.label: Forest lost in the Ecuadorian Amazon in 2022

source.title: MAAP #200: State of the Amazon in 2023 (Amazon Conservation)
source.quote: deforestation in the Ecuadorian Amazon was the highest on record in 2022 (18,902 hectares), up a striking 80% since 2021

rows.explainer: Primary forest lost in the Ecuadorian Amazon in its worst recorded year; averaged with 2021 below, so the baseline is a run-rate (Convention 9).

rows.label: Rise in Ecuadorian Amazon forest loss from 2021 to 2022

source.title: MAAP #200: State of the Amazon in 2023 (Amazon Conservation)
source.quote: deforestation in the Ecuadorian Amazon was the highest on record in 2022 (18,902 hectares), up a striking 80% since 2021

rows.explainer: With the 2022 figure, gives 2021's loss (about 10,500 hectares), so the rate below is the two years' average rather than the record year.

rows.label: Forest in the Ecuadorian Amazon

source.title: Timber Trade Portal, Ecuador: country context (FAO 2015)
source.quote: The majority of forests - approximately 9.9 million ha (nearly 80%) - is in the Amazon region.

rows.explainer: FAO's 2015 figure; MapBiomas's later count implies about 7.5 million hectares, the low end.

rows.label: Loss rate in the Biocorridor's lands relative to the Ecuadorian Amazon's average
rows.explainer: The Biocorridor covers both remote forest (lower pressure than average) and corridors chosen because they are threatened (higher). We take the regional average (1), with a range from half to twice it.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: yearly forest loss rate without the protection (2021-2022 average)
rows.explainer: The average of 2021 and 2022 losses over the forest area: about 0.15% a year at the best guesses. The record year alone (0.19%) is within site_vs_regional_loss's range.

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon: forest a year that would be lost without the protection
rows.explainer: The counted hectares × the region's loss rate: the loss the protection works against, before its effect (deal_counterfactual_adj).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon: CO₂ at risk over the years counted, discounted
Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per person per year
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the largest matched study, Naidoo et al. (2019, Science Advances, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aav3006: more than 60,000 households near or far from 600 protected areas in 34 countries): households near protected areas with tourism had a 17% higher wealth index and were 16% less likely to be poor, with no evidence of harm on average, though protection sometimes cuts people off from land and fish. A wealth index isn't consumption, the Biocorridor and the marine plans bring little tourism, and gains build slowly, so our best guess is a small gain, 0.5% of consumption a year (ln 0.005), with a range from a 2% loss to a 4% gain.

rows.label: Deals' local incomes: units of value over the years counted, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × the yearly gain in ln(consumption) × the discounted years the deals are counted for × the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: Land bought: yearly chance a parcel would have been developed or cleared without the purchase
rows.explainer: TNC buys land under threat of development, logging or farming, mostly in the US. Our guess, 0.4% a year (0.1-1.5%), is a few times the US average loss of natural land to development (about 0.1-0.2% a year in the USDA's National Resources Inventory), for parcels chosen because they are at risk. Small next to the Amazon branch either way.

rows.label: Land bought: CO₂ released per hectare converted
rows.explainer: A mix of temperate forest (several hundred tonnes of CO₂ in trees and soil, not all of it released on conversion), grassland and wetland (tens of tonnes, mostly soil carbon): 150 tonnes a hectare (30-400).

rows.label: Land bought: hectares a year that would be converted without the purchase
Land bought: years counted, discounted (no wait: ownership protects at once)
rows.explainer: A purchase protects from the day it closes, so there is no wait; it counts the shared years a win counts (another trust or agency might have bought the land later), not perpetuity.

rows.label: Land bought: CO₂ at risk over the years counted, discounted
Wellbeing: life satisfaction gained per person per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Life-satisfaction points (0-10) a year for someone who gains access to nature: studies of green space find small effects (hundredths of a point); only reached at the range's high end, since nature_people is 0 at its best guess.

rows.label: Protection policy: yearly forest loss rate on those hectares without protection
rows.explainer: Anchored on the Ecuadorian Amazon's 0.15% a year (amazon_loss_rate) and the tropics' primary-forest loss of 3.7 million hectares a year over roughly a billion hectares (about 0.4%); policy work targets threatened frontiers, so 0.3% (0.1-1%).

rows.label: Protection policy: forest a year that would be lost without the protection
Protection policy: CO₂ at risk over the years counted, discounted
Clean energy: lifetime of a solar project
rows.explainer: Solar farms are financed and warrantied over 20-30 years; 25 turns the Neyveli lifetime figure into tonnes a year.

rows.label: Clean energy: electricity a US home uses in a year

source.title: US Energy Information Administration, FAQ: How much electricity does an American home use?
source.quote: In 2022, the average annual amount of electricity sold to (purchased by) a U.S. residential electric-utility customer was 10,791 kilowatthours (kWh)

rows.explainer: 10,791 kWh in 2022, in MWh.

rows.label: Clean energy: CO₂ per MWh of grid power a new solar project displaces (Appalachia)
rows.explainer: New solar in the Southeast displaces mostly gas and some coal at the margin: about 0.4 t a MWh for gas, 0.9-1.0 for coal (EPA eGRID's output rates), the regions' averages 0.4-0.5. Our guess is 0.6 (0.35-0.9).

rows.label: Clean energy: CO₂ a year the year's named projects avoid
rows.explainer: Neyveli (about 47,000 t a year) and the Appalachian projects (about 39,000 t a year): about 86,000 t a year.

rows.label: Clean energy (mine-land projects): CO₂ a year, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The named projects only; the pathway's siting maps and policy work are their own branch (siting_).

rows.label: Clean energy: wait until the projects generate
rows.explainer: Neyveli came online in September 2025, the Appalachian projects are announced plans: about two years on average from the year's spending (0-4).

rows.label: Clean energy: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: A project TNC helped site would mostly be built somewhere later anyway: the shared years a win counts, after the wait, discounted.

rows.label: Clean energy: CO₂ over the years counted, discounted, before adjustments
Siting maps: share of the year the capacity generates at full output
rows.explainer: Utility solar runs at about 18-25% of its rated output over a year, onshore wind 25-35%; a solar-heavy mix, 22% (15-35%).

rows.label: Hours in a year

source.title: US Energy Information Administration, Glossary: capacity factor
source.quote: The ratio of the electrical energy produced by a generating unit for the period of time considered to the electrical energy that could have been produced at continuous full power operation during the same period.

rows.explainer: 365 × 24 hours: capacity (GW) × the capacity factor × the hours gives the energy in GWh.

rows.label: Siting maps: CO₂ per MWh of the power the new capacity displaces (mostly India)
rows.explainer: India's grid emits about 0.7 t CO₂ a MWh (its Central Electricity Authority's baseline, mostly coal); Europe's displaced power less. 0.7 (0.4-0.95).

rows.label: Siting maps: CO₂ a year the planned capacity would displace, before adjustments
rows.explainer: GW × capacity factor × hours × 1,000 (GWh to MWh) × t CO₂ a MWh; the share brought forward by the maps is siting_counterfactual_adj.

rows.label: Siting maps: wait until planned capacity generates
rows.explainer: From a siting plan to a project online takes three to five years (Gumber et al. 2024, Applied Energy: commissioning times rising); three (1-5).

rows.label: Siting maps: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: Capacity brought forward counts the shared years a win counts, after the wait.

rows.label: Siting maps: CO₂ over the years counted, discounted, before adjustments
Pará: forest cleared, PRODES 2023 (August 2022 to July 2023)

source.title: INPE, Nota técnica: taxa consolidada de desmatamento PRODES Amazônia 2024 (July 2025)

rows.explainer: 3,299 km², Brazil's official satellite count of clear-cutting in the state.

rows.label: Pará: forest cleared, PRODES 2024 (August 2023 to July 2024)

source.title: INPE, Nota técnica: taxa consolidada de desmatamento PRODES Amazônia 2024 (July 2025)

rows.explainer: 2,395 km², 37% of the Legal Amazon's clearing that year.

rows.label: Pará: forest cleared a year (2023-2024 average)
rows.explainer: A two-year run-rate (Convention 9); clearing has fallen fast since 2021, which the range of zdc_implementation_adj and the wait carry.

rows.label: Pará: share of clearing driven by cattle ranching

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Annual Report 2025
source.page: Protecting the Amazon, Feeding the Planet, p. 15
source.quote: Cattle ranching alone accounts for more than 90% of clear-cutting in the Amazon.

rows.explainer: TNC's figure for the Amazon; the low end allows for soy, mining and land speculation in Pará's share.

rows.label: Cattle traceability: share of cattle-driven clearing removed when every buyer applies zero-deforestation rules

source.title: Levy et al. (2023), Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon could be halved by scaling up the implementation of zero-deforestation cattle commitments, Global Environmental Change 80, 102671
source.quote: had all firms adopted and implemented an effective ZDC, cattle-driven deforestation could have dropped by 24,000 ± 13,000 km2 (51 ± 28%)

rows.explainer: From farmers' exposure to zero-deforestation buyers across the Brazilian Amazon, 2010-2018: the G4 agreement cut cattle-driven clearing by 15 ± 8%, and full adoption and implementation would have cut it by 51 ± 28% (the range). Pará's Sustainable Cattle Program makes traceability of every animal mandatory for all producers (the decree: the whole herd by December 2026; TNC: full compliance by 2030), the full-adoption case; how much of that is delivered is zdc_implementation_adj. The effect is against no traceability rule, net of the other policies of the period; leakage onto unmonitored land (Alix-Garcia et al. 2017, doi 10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2017.08.009, found the early agreements' gains offset on later-registered properties) is a negative share in zdc_unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Cattle traceability: forest a year the full rule keeps in Pará
rows.explainer: About 130,000 hectares a year at the best guesses; TNC's own estimate for the policy is 110,000 (annual report 2025, p. 17), a cross-check.

rows.label: Cattle traceability: years of work behind the rule (a year's share of the win)
rows.explainer: Pará launched the programme in 2023 after years of TNC's work with the state and the industry (TNC calls it the latest step in 20 years of work on deforestation-free farming), and implementation continues to 2030. As a past average (Convention 11), a year's spending gets one year's share of the win: the rule's years of preparation and roll-out, about six (3-10).

rows.label: Cattle traceability: wait until the rule binds
rows.explainer: The state decree sets animals in transit tagged by the end of 2025 and the whole herd by December 2026 (Congresso em Foco, 31 March 2025, congressoemfoco.com.br/noticia/107373); TNC's annual report gives 2030 for full mandatory compliance for all producers. The model uses the decree as the start and the slow roll-out so far as reason to expect the rule to bind on clearing later: on average about three years from the year's spending (1-5, the low end the decree's schedule, the high end TNC's 2030).

rows.label: Cattle traceability: years counted, discounted
Cattle traceability: CO₂ kept, credited to the year, discounted
rows.explainer: Hectares kept a year × the tropics' CO₂ per hectare × the discounted years counted ÷ the years of work behind the rule. The hectares are already the avoided loss, so zdc_counterfactual_adj is 1 (one question per adjustment).

rows.label: Gran Chaco: woodland cleared, 2000-2012

source.title: Fehlenberg et al. (2017), The role of soybean production as an underlying driver of deforestation in the South American Chaco, Global Environmental Change 45, 24-34
source.quote: the Chaco, a 110 million ha ecoregion extending into Argentina, Bolivia, and Paraguay, with about 8 million ha of deforestation in 2000–2012

rows.explainer: Clearing across Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay. A later run-rate is no lower on the evidence: Argentina's clearing fell after its 2007 forest law, but Baumann et al. (2022, Environmental Research Letters, doi 10.1088/1748-9326/ac8b9a) count 19.3 million hectares converted 1985-2020, about 550,000 a year, with a surge after 2019; the range of conv_soy_share carries the difference.

rows.label: Gran Chaco: years in that period

source.title: Fehlenberg et al. (2017), Global Environmental Change 45, 24-34
source.quote: about 8 million ha of deforestation in 2000–2012

rows.explainer: 2000 to 2012 inclusive.

rows.label: Gran Chaco: share of clearing the soy supply chains TNC works on can reach
rows.explainer: Fehlenberg et al. find soy a direct driver in the Argentine Chaco and an indirect one (pushing cattle) in Bolivia and Paraguay; cattle are the main proximate cause in Paraguay. TNC's zero-conversion work (VISEC, Argentina's soy traceability platform; the CCAT fund for farmers who don't clear) reaches the Argentine soy chain: 30% of the region's clearing (10-60%).

rows.label: Zero-conversion commodities: woodland a year the full rules would keep
rows.explainer: Clearing a year × the share the soy chain can reach × the effect of zero-deforestation buying when all buyers apply it (Levy et al. 2023, the same evidence as the cattle rule; voluntary soy traceability is weaker, in conv_implementation_adj).

rows.label: Gran Chaco: CO₂ released per hectare of dry woodland cleared
rows.explainer: Dry Chaco woodland holds far less carbon than rainforest: about 30-90 tonnes of carbon a hectare above and below ground, plus soil carbon lost on clearing (× 44/12: 100-350 t CO₂). 200 t CO₂ (100-350), against the tropics' 650 for rainforest.

rows.label: Zero-conversion commodities: years of work behind the year's commitments
rows.explainer: VISEC and the CCAT fund took years of work with traders, banks and farmers; as a past average a year's spending gets one year's share (Convention 11): five years (3-10).

rows.label: Zero-conversion commodities: wait until the rules bind on clearing
rows.explainer: Traceability and finance take a few years to reach the farms that clear: two (1-5).

rows.label: Zero-conversion commodities: years counted, discounted
Zero-conversion commodities: CO₂ kept, credited to the year, discounted, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Hectares kept a year × CO₂ per hectare × the discounted years ÷ the years of work. Dry woodland, not tropical rainforest: no pandemic-risk step (the shared rate is per hectare of tropical forest).

rows.label: Foodscapes: soil carbon a hectare under cover crops gains a year, as CO₂

source.title: Poeplau & Don (2015), Carbon sequestration in agricultural soils via cultivation of cover crops – A meta-analysis, Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 200, 33-41
source.quote: an annual change rate of 0.32 ± 0.08 Mg ha−1 yr−1 in a mean soil depth of 22 cm

rows.explainer: Poeplau & Don's meta-analysis of 139 plots: 0.32 t of carbon a hectare a year (× 44/12: 1.2 t CO₂). A re-analysis that kept only sound trials found 0.03 t C (Chaplot & Smith 2023, Global Change Biology, doi 10.1111/gcb.16917: 0.1 t CO₂). Our best guess is between, 0.7 t CO₂ (0.1-1.5).

rows.label: Foodscapes: years the practice is kept, discounted
Foodscapes: years a farm keeps the practice
rows.explainer: Many farmers drop cover crops once payments end, and the carbon gained comes back out when they do; eight years on average (3-20).

rows.label: Foodscapes: share of the soil carbon gained that stays stored
rows.explainer: The shared value of a tonne is for a permanent tonne. Soil carbon gained under cover crops comes back out within years when farmers drop the practice or till again, and many drop it when payments end; our guess is that 30% of the gain stays (0-100%).

rows.label: Foodscapes: CO₂ stored for good over the years kept, discounted, before adjustments
Crop residue burned per hectare a year before the programme
rows.explainer: Punjab burned about 20.3 million tonnes of residue in 2017-18 (Singh et al. 2020, below) over about 3 million hectares of rice and 3.5 million of wheat; a rice-wheat farm that burns produces 6-7 tonnes of rice straw a hectare and burns most of it. 4 tonnes a hectare a year (2-7).

rows.label: PRANA: reduction in residue burning among the programme's farmers (midline)

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Provide Food & Water Global Priority: 2025 Year in Review
source.quote: From February to April 2025, we conducted a midline assessment, which indicated a 25% reduction in residue burning

rows.explainer: TNC's midline assessment, against the programme's baseline, without a comparison group: statewide burning has fallen too (prana_counterfactual_adj). The range is ours.

rows.label: India: deaths a year from the fine particles of crop-residue burning (2003-2019 average)

source.title: Lan et al. (2022), Air quality impacts of crop residue burning in India and mitigation alternatives, Nature Communications 13, 6537 (PMC9663555)
source.quote: we estimate 69,000 (95% CI: 57,000–80,000) total premature mortalities on average across India

rows.explainer: An adjoint chemical-transport model of India's air. The abstract's 44,000-98,000 is the spread between years; the paper's 2003-2019 average is about 69,000 (95% interval 57,000-80,000), which we use. A smaller study (Saharan et al. 2024, Environmental Pollution, doi 10.1016/j.envpol.2024.124013) puts the Indo-Gangetic Plain's deaths at about 18,000, within the low end of the combined range through prana_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Share of those deaths from burning in Punjab and Haryana

source.title: Lan et al. (2022), Nature Communications 13, 6537 (PMC9663555)
source.quote: This means 380 (95% CI: 320–450) and 45 (95% CI: 37–52) averted premature deaths

rows.explainer: From the paper's sensitivities: a 1% cut in post-monsoon burning emissions averts about 380 deaths for Punjab's and 45 for Haryana's, 0.57% and 0.065% of India's impact, so the two states carry about 62% of it (55-70%). Punjab's tonnes do about four times the harm of Haryana's; PRANA's farmers are in both, in shares TNC doesn't publish, so the two-state average is used.

rows.label: Punjab: crop residue burned in the field, 2017-18

source.title: Singh et al. (2020), A high-resolution emission inventory of air pollutants from primary crop residue burning over Northern India based on VIIRS thermal anomalies, Environmental Pollution 266, 115132
source.quote: An estimated 20.3 Mt and 9.6 Mt of crop residue were burned in Punjab and Haryana

rows.label: Haryana: crop residue burned in the field, 2017-18

source.title: Singh et al. (2020), A high-resolution emission inventory of air pollutants from primary crop residue burning over Northern India based on VIIRS thermal anomalies, Environmental Pollution 266, 115132
source.quote: An estimated 20.3 Mt and 9.6 Mt of crop residue were burned in Punjab and Haryana

rows.label: Deaths per tonne of residue burned in Punjab and Haryana
rows.explainer: The two states' share of the deaths over the residue they burn: about 1.4 deaths per thousand tonnes. Lan et al.'s years and Singh et al.'s are close but not the same; burning has fallen since, and a tonne's harm depends on the wind and the hour (Lan et al.), both in the ranges.

rows.label: PRANA: residue a year no longer burned by the programme's farmers, before adjustments
PRANA: deaths a year averted, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Farmers × hectares × residue each hectare burned × the share no longer burned × deaths per tonne. The year's burning avoided by the farmers in the programme counts against the year's spending (a steady programme's yearly flow, Convention 3); later years are later spending's.

rows.label: PRANA: value of a death from air pollution, by the ages these deaths come at
rows.explainer: The shared ages of air-pollution deaths (GBD 2023, mostly over 50) × the shared value of a death in each band × the value-of-a-life slider: the same value the site gives every air-pollution death.

rows.label: PRANA: units of value a year, before adjustments
rows.explainer: One year's deaths averted, valued; the illness that comes with the smoke is a positive share in prana_unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Methane and nitrous oxide from burning a tonne of crop residue, as CO₂e
rows.explainer: The CO₂ from burning straw is regrown the next season and isn't counted; the methane (about 2.7 g a kg burned) and nitrous oxide (about 0.07 g a kg) are, at 28 and 265 times CO₂: about 0.09 t CO₂e a tonne (IPCC 2006 Guidelines, Volume 4, Table 2.5, agricultural residues). 0.1 (0.05-0.2).

rows.label: PRANA: methane and nitrous oxide not emitted in the year, before adjustments
rows.explainer: One year's residue not burned × the non-CO₂ emissions a tonne; counted in tonnes in its own unit (Convention 13).

rows.label: Restoration: CO₂ a regrowing hectare takes up a year
rows.explainer: Cook-Patton et al. (2020, Nature, doi 10.1038/s41586-020-2686-x) map a hundredfold spread in natural regrowth rates by place, lowest in dry and cold forests; temperate regrowth takes up about 0.5-1 t of carbon a hectare a year (2-4 t CO₂). Young tropical regrowth in the Amazon takes up 1.3-3.0 t C (Heinrich et al. 2021, Nature Communications, doi 10.1038/s41467-021-22050-1: about 5-11 t CO₂), the high end. TNC's regrowth is mostly temperate and dry forest and catchments: 2.5 t CO₂ (0.5-8).

rows.label: Restoration: years a restored hectare keeps taking up carbon
rows.explainer: Regrowth takes up carbon fastest in its first 20-40 years (Robinson et al. 2025, Nature Climate Change, doi 10.1038/s41558-025-02355-5: peak rates at about 30 years); fire, drought and reclearing end some early. 20 years (10-40).

rows.label: Restoration: years of uptake, discounted
Restoration: CO₂ taken up over the years counted, discounted, before adjustments
Fisheries: yearly gain in ln(consumption) per person
rows.explainer: Anchored on matched comparisons: communities near marine protected areas in the Mesoamerican reef had higher incomes and food security than those far away (Nowakowski et al. 2023, Nature Sustainability, doi 10.1038/s41893-023-01150-4); co-managed small-scale fisheries raise catches (d'Armengol et al. 2018, Global Environmental Change, doi 10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2018.07.009); new restrictions cut fishers' incomes in the first years in the Philippines (Samonte et al. 2016). Monitoring industrial fleets reaches small-scale fishers' catches only indirectly: 0.5% of consumption (−0.5% to +3%).

rows.label: Fisheries: wait until the gains come
rows.explainer: Monitoring has to be installed and fish stocks take years to respond: three years (1-6).

rows.label: Fisheries: years counted, discounted
Fisheries: units of value over the years counted, before adjustments
Adaptation: yearly gain in ln(consumption) per person from flood and storm losses avoided
rows.explainer: Anchors: mangroves avert about $65 billion of flood damage a year for 15 million people (Menéndez et al. 2020, Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-020-61136-6) and coral reefs about $4 billion (Beck et al. 2018, Nature Communications, doi 10.1038/s41467-018-04568-z), much of it property. A project adds a small increment of protection to habitat that already exists (faster reef repair after a storm, a restored mangrove strip): 0.2% of consumption a year (0-1%).

rows.label: Adaptation: wait until the protection works
rows.explainer: Insurance protects from its first season, but restored mangroves and repaired reefs take years to grow into a barrier: two years on average (0-5).

rows.label: Adaptation: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: Insurance schemes and restored habitat are won and set up once: the shared years a win counts, after the wait, discounted.

rows.label: Adaptation: units of value over the years counted, before adjustments
Healthy years a person gains a year (not used)
rows.explainer: Not reached: health_people is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of disabling pain spared per animal-year (negative if more)
rows.explainer: Not reached (wild_animal_years is 0). On Ambitious Impact's pain scale the sign is unknown for a protected forest, hence the range across 0.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: deaths in a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance above is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a pandemic as deadly as COVID-19
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about 2% a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drives
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than 30% of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: IPBES's land-use change includes farming expansion, settlement and wildlife trade as well as clearing tropical forest. Anchor: Allen et al. (2017, Nature Communications, doi 10.1038/s41467-017-00923-8) find emerging-disease hotspots best predicted by tropical forest regions with high mammal diversity undergoing land-use change, so clearing tropical forest is a large part, not all, of the land-use risk. We take half of it as scaling with tropical forest loss, in proportion to the hectares lost (10-100%); Dobson et al. (Science, 2020) argue for cutting deforestation as pandemic prevention but give no dose-response. The least grounded number in the model, and through the cattle rule's branch it carries much of the result.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly cut in the chance of a COVID-scale pandemic per hectare of tropical forest kept a year
rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept. No study has measured this dose; the least grounded number in the model.

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: COVID-19's excess deaths were mostly of older people and few of young children; a different pathogen could hit children harder (the range's top). Anchored on WHO's excess-mortality age profile (Msemburi et al. 2023, Nature: most excess deaths over 60).

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: School-age children were the least affected group in COVID-19; up to 5% for a pathogen like the 1918 influenza.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: About 15% of COVID-19's adult excess deaths were under 50 (WHO's age profile, most deaths over 60); up to 40% for a pathogen that kills young adults (1918 influenza). The rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number. Future generations are the next two rows.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: 0: the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above. The tiny high end allows for lasting damage.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk (Ecuador Amazon deal (forest)): pandemic risk cut × years, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The tropical forest this branch keeps a year (before its counterfactual, which its adjustments apply) × the risk cut per hectare × the branch's discounted years.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk (Ecuador Amazon deal (forest)): pandemic deaths averted, valued, before adjustments
Catastrophic risk (protection policy): pandemic risk cut × years, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The tropical forest this branch keeps a year (before its counterfactual, which its adjustments apply) × the risk cut per hectare × the branch's discounted years.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk (protection policy): pandemic deaths averted, valued, before adjustments
Catastrophic risk (deforestation-free cattle (Pará)): pandemic risk cut × years, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The tropical forest this branch keeps a year (before its counterfactual, which its adjustments apply) × the risk cut per hectare × the branch's discounted years.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk (deforestation-free cattle (Pará)): pandemic deaths averted, valued, before adjustments
Ecuador Amazon deal: units of value (pandemic risk), before adjustments
Protection policy: units of value (pandemic risk), before adjustments
Cattle traceability: units of value (pandemic risk), before adjustments
Catastrophic risk: yearly cut in the chance of a COVID-scale pandemic credited to the year (for reading)
rows.formula: (deal_risk_years * deal_credit + prot_risk_years * prot_credit + zdc_risk_years * zdc_credit) / protection_years
rows.explainer: The forest branches' risk-years after their adjustments, per discounted year of protection: about one in a hundred billion a year. For reading and the bounds check; the branches' uov rows carry it.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future years of healthy life kept, discounted
rows.formula: (deal_risk_years * deal_credit + prot_risk_years * prot_credit + zdc_risk_years * zdc_credit) * future_share_lost * @catastrophe.world_population_long_run / $discount_rate
rows.explainer: Every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take (the long-run world population × the share lost), discounted for ever at the shared rate; 0 at the best guess (future_share_lost). Already credited by branch.

rows.label: The year's ocean deals: TNC's share of their resources
rows.explainer: The Bahamas' debt conversion is paid for by the country's debt savings with a guarantee and insurance from others; TNC structured it and leads the marine planning (as in the Seychelles, where it led the marine spatial plan). A larger role than in the Amazon deal: 10% (3-30%).

rows.label: Proceeds from sales of conservation land and easements, FY2025

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)
source.page: Consolidated statements of cash flows, p. 8
source.quote: Proceeds from sale of conservation land and easements 91,545

rows.explainer: TNC sells much of the land it buys to government agencies and other conservation owners, who pay part of the cost.

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Ecuador Amazon deal: how far to trust the effect figures: the 41% protected-area effect is a global average from matched (not randomised) comparisons and may not hold for the Biocorridor's mix of new and existing areas (×0.9); the CO₂ per hectare is the tropics' average and the loss rate a two-year regional average, not the Biocorridor's own (×0.9). Together 0.8 (0.5-1), in line with the evidence discounts on land-carbon estimates in Founders Pledge's forest work on the site (coalition-for-rainforest-nations-founders-pledge).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The share of the forest at risk that protection keeps (Wolf et al. 2021's 41%): applied once here, since deal_tco2e and the pandemic rows count the forest at risk before protection.

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): TNC's share of the resources
rows.explainer: The Biocorridor is paid for by about $460 million over 17 years from Ecuador's debt savings, made possible by an IDB guarantee, DFC political-risk insurance and Bank of America's financing, with Indigenous nations co-designing and the government delivering. TNC designed the deal and gives technical support; its own cost isn't published but is likely in the tens of millions over the years of preparation and support. Its share of all resources is about 5% (2-15%). This is TNC's share of the deal's own resources over its life, not of TNC's yearly deal budget (that is in the cost).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): share delivered
rows.explainer: The share of the Biocorridor's targets (1.8 million hectares newly protected, 4.6 million better managed) we expect to be delivered over its years: such programmes often fall behind on declarations and enforcement. 70% (40-90%), anchored on Brazil's ARPA programme, the model for these deals, which met its area targets with uneven management.

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Negative: leakage, clearing pushed onto unprotected land (studies of protected areas find from none to about 40% of the avoided loss displaced). Positive: the Biocorridor's 18,000 km of river protections, water regulation and flood protection. Net −10% (−40% to +20%).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: TNC reports the deal's hectares, but the forest it keeps is the regional loss rate × a global protection effect, not measured for the Biocorridor; nobody measures the deal's outcomes against a comparison. The shared missing-data discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): product of the adjustments
Ecuador Amazon deal (forest): share of the branch's outcome credited to the year's dollar
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × (1 + its unmodelled effects) × the next-dollar slider: this branch's outcome is a won deal, rule or policy set against a year's spending, a past average (Convention 11).

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Naidoo et al.'s matched comparisons are observational and of protected areas with tourism; the gain here is already a judgment below their effect. 0.8 (0.5-1), as for the deal's forest.

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the income gain is a matched comparison against similar people without protection, so it is already net of what would have happened anyway; whether the deals would have come anyway is the years counted.

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): TNC's share of the resources
rows.explainer: TNC's share of each deal's resources, weighted by the people in it: the Amazon deal's share (deal_attribution_share) and the ocean deals' (ocean_attribution_share).

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): share delivered
rows.explainer: The share of the deals' plans delivered over their years, as for the Amazon deal's forest (deal_implementation_adj): 70% (40-90%).

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: 0: harms to people who lose access are already inside the gain's range across 0.

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: the people reached and the income gain are judgments; no study of these deals' communities. The shared missing-data discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: The year's deals (local incomes): product of the adjustments
The year's deals (local incomes): share of the branch's outcome credited to the year's dollar
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × (1 + its unmodelled effects) × the next-dollar slider: this branch's outcome is a won deal, rule or policy set against a year's spending, a past average (Convention 11).

rows.label: Land bought: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Validity only (that the figures are judgments is the missing-data step): a purchase or easement stops development by law, so the chain is direct; some parcels were less threatened than chosen for. 0.9 (0.6-1).

rows.label: Land bought: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Owning the land, or an easement on it in perpetuity, stops development almost entirely; we leave 10% for later sales, swaps and weak enforcement (range 70-100%).

rows.label: Land bought: TNC's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Agencies and other buyers pay back part of what TNC spends on land: TNC's share is what it keeps paying, one minus sales over purchases (about 56% in FY2025, a steady-state reading, since the year's sales are of land bought earlier).

rows.label: Land bought: share delivered
rows.explainer: 1: the purchases closed (the audited cash flow); delivery is not in doubt.

rows.label: Land bought: effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Negative: development pushed onto nearby land. Positive: water, flood protection and recreation on the land, and the year's gifts of land ($48.1 million of contributed land and easements, not counted in reach). Net 0 (−20% to +30%).

rows.label: Land bought: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: TNC reports what it paid, not the hectares; the land's risk of conversion and carbon are judgments. The shared missing-data discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: Land bought: product of the adjustments
Land bought: share of the branch's outcome credited to the year's dollar

rows.explainer: The midline compares with the programme's baseline, not with similar farmers, and burning fell across both states far more than 25% over the same years: satellite fire counts in Punjab fell from about 71,000 in 2021, PRANA's first season, to about 11,000 in 2024 (Punjab Remote Sensing Centre, as reported by the Press Trust of India), and over Punjab and Haryana by half or more from 2015 to 2023 (Mangaraj et al. 2025), under bans, machinery subsidies and enforcement. Fire counts overstate the fall in burnt area (farmers burn after the satellite passes), but the statewide trend covers most or all of the programme's 25%. Our guess is that 15% of it is the programme's own (5-50%), the high end for its influence on how the subsidised machines get used.

The government's crop-residue-management scheme released about ₹3,300 crore to Punjab (₹1,531 crore), Haryana (₹1,006 crore), Uttar Pradesh and Delhi from 2018-19, for more than 2.95 lakh machines (Rajya Sabha reply, February 2024); at the counterfactual's 15% the part due to PRANA would be a modest share of it.
